lesson.title: The Signal That Never Repeats
lesson.summary: An aperiodic signal never settles into an exact repeating pattern, no matter how long you observe it, which is actually the normal case for most real-world signals like speech, transients, and noise.
lesson.body:
An aperiodic, or non-periodic, signal is any signal for which no period T exists such that x(t + T) = x(t) holds for all t. This is not some rare exception to periodic signals, it is closer to the default condition of real-world signals. A single voltage pulse from pressing a button, a snippet of recorded speech, the voltage across a capacitor as it discharges, thermal noise picked up on a long wire: none of these ever return to repeating their exact prior shape.

A capacitor discharging through a resistor gives a clean worked example of an aperiodic signal with a perfectly well-defined mathematical description. Its voltage follows v(t) = V0 e^(-t / RC). Take V0 = 5 V and RC = 1 ms. At t = 0, v = 5 V. At t = 1 ms, one time constant has passed, and v = 5 x e^-1 = 5 x 0.3679 = 1.84 V. At t = 2 ms, v = 5 x e^-2 = 5 x 0.1353 = 0.677 V. At t = 5 ms, v = 5 x e^-5 = 5 x 0.00674 = 0.0337 V. The voltage keeps falling toward zero and never comes back up to revisit 1.84 V or any earlier value, so there is no T that makes this waveform repeat: it is aperiodic, even though its shape is completely predictable and describable in closed form.

Periodicity can also hide in unexpected places, or fail to appear where it looks like it should. A sum of two sinusoids whose frequencies have an irrational ratio to each other, say 1 Hz and the square root of 2 Hz, never realigns into an exact repeat no matter how long you wait, so despite looking wave-like and orderly, it is technically aperiodic. In practice, engineers often care only about apparent repetition over some finite observation window, but the strict mathematical distinction still matters, because periodic and aperiodic signals call for different analysis tools. A periodic signal decomposes into a Fourier series: a discrete list of frequency components at the fundamental and its harmonics, the subject of the next few chapters. An aperiodic signal instead requires the Fourier transform, which produces a continuous spectrum rather than a discrete list, a tool for a later chapter in this sequence.
